# 1.1 Valence: good and bad {#sec-valence}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.1"></div>

The animal of the previous stage steers by reflex. What it sees is wired, through a small ganglion, straight to
its motor neurons. It has no way of knowing what happened after it bit something.

This stage gives it that. It adds a handful of neurons that stand for *this is good* and *this is bad*, and puts
food in the world that is bad to eat.

## The world: two kinds of berry are poison

There are now six kinds of berry bush instead of four. They look alike, in the way that different berries look
alike: each kind has the shape of a bush and its own colour.

Four kinds are food. Two are poison, and always the same two. Eating a poison berry empties the stomach by about
as much as a good berry fills it, and it hurts for a moment.

Because the same two kinds are poison in every life, nothing has to be learned during a life. Which colours to
avoid can be inherited. Learning it within a life is the subject of a later stage.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.1"></div>

## The biology: valence

In small animals, most sensory neurons fall into two classes. Some respond to things worth approaching, such as
the smell of food. Others respond to things worth avoiding, such as a harmful chemical or a hard touch on the
nose. The two classes converge onto a few interneurons that bias the animal towards carrying on or turning away.

*Valence* is the name for this sorting of the world into good and bad. In the worm *C. elegans*, a much-studied
animal with 302 neurons, harmful stimuli do two things at once: they trigger a turn, and they stop the pumping of
the throat with which the worm feeds. Max Bennett argues that this sorting is what the first brains were for.

The worm is only a stand-in. The animal that this chapter is about, the common ancestor of animals with a left
and a right side, left no nervous system to look at.

## The circuit

Five new groups of neurons, each with a meaning that is fixed by its wiring:

- **`valence_app`**, the *appetitive* cells: active when something is good. The sense of taste is hard-wired to
  them, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
- **`valence_av`**, the *aversive* cells: active when something is bad. Pain is hard-wired to them, and reaches
  the brain nowhere else.
- **`grasp`**, a *motor programme*: when it fires, the animal bites what is in front of it.
- **`no_touch`**, a *gate*: an inhibitory cell that is active whenever nothing is directly ahead, and holds
  `grasp` shut.
- **`no_feed`**: an inhibitory pair driven by the aversive cells, which blocks the bite.

Taste and pain are *unconditioned* signals: they mean good and bad without any experience. But they arrive only
after the bite. To act in time, the value cells also get input from the eyes, and that input is evolved. Over
generations, the look of a poison berry comes to excite the aversive cells before anything has been eaten.

Value does not move the animal by itself. The appetitive cells excite `grasp`, but `grasp` can only fire when
`no_touch` is silent, that is, when something is within reach. Releasing an action by switching off its
inhibition is called *disinhibition*, and it is a common arrangement in real nervous systems. Here it makes a
value turn into the right action for the situation: bite when the good thing is in front of the mouth, and not
before.

The aversive cells do what the worm does. They drive the motor neurons for turning, and through `no_feed` they
shut down biting.

## Watching it work

Below is one animal from the last generation, around the moment it bites a poison berry.

Step through it one tick at a time. At the bite, nothing in the brain has changed yet: the pain arrives with the
next tick. Then the `pain` sense is on, both aversive cells fire, `no_feed` switches on and `grasp` falls silent.
The animal turns away. A few ticks later the pain has faded and it is eating again.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.1" data-example="bad_berry"></div>

Nothing was learned here. The animal will react in the same way the next time. What stops it from biting poison
often is the evolved input from the eyes, which acts before the bite.

## Results

### Is main worse than control?

The control is the brain of stage 1.0 in this world. It cannot feel pain or taste at all, so it can only avoid
poison if evolution happens to wire the look of the poison berries to turning away.

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.1"></div>

The three rows measure the same thing with less and less noise. The first is taken from the generations as they
ran. The second gives every final population the same eight worlds. In the third, main and control animals live
together and compete for the same bushes, so a difference cannot come from one population having had an easier
world.

### Is the circuit used?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.1"></div>

Read this chart region by region. A short bar means the animals depended on that region. A bar near 100 means
they did as well without it, and three dots far apart mean the seeds disagree.

::: {.callout-note title="What did not work: appetite on a full stomach"}
In the runs where animals are born with a full stomach, the aversive side is used and the appetitive side is not:
silencing `valence_app`, `no_touch` or `grasp` leaves the animals as well off as before. The reason is that the
appetitive side makes the animal bite whenever food is in reach, hungry or not, and a bite on a full stomach
earns nothing under a fitness that counts being well fed. Nothing in this brain can sense hunger yet.

This note describes the born-full runs. If the chart above shows those three bars well below 100, the stage has
been rerun with animals born a quarter full, and this note is due for rewriting.
:::
